title: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
description: Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.Raids took place in 12 prov
body: Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values. One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL. Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community. Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office. In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL. The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country. Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years. "The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

schema.headline: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists

title: Will record donations to Reform be a moment of political change?
description: When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking £36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback
body: When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking £36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback.The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away.In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper.Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team.But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest.Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised £30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals.This extra £72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country.In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important.Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election.It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine.Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely.Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations.Labour is already planning to introduce a cap on the amount of money a British citizen living overseas can donate.There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes.The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations.Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules.Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers.The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger.Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate.But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed.

schema.headline: Will record donations to Reform be a moment of political change?

title: Tom English: Derek McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker
description: Fifty-five minutes into this Rangers romp at Ibrox, Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney stood beside each other in the Celtic technical area, chin-stroki
body: Fifty-five minutes into this Rangers romp at Ibrox, Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney stood beside each other in the Celtic technical area, chin-stroking, head-scratching, pointing, waving, drowning.To them, in this moment, this Premier Sports Cup quarter-final must have felt like a surreal and nightmarish occasion - and it was only 1-0 at the time. Rangers had really only started to wreak their havoc.Such was Rangers' dominance, their complete owning of their visitors in every conceivable category, the Celtic managerial brains trust seemed just as lost as every one of their players on the field. Man for man, Rangers won every battle, not for 45 minutes but for the full ninety.No away fans, of course. Not that that had anything to do with it. Being locked out of Ibrox might have seemed like a curse to Celtic folk. In the end, it must have felt like the greatest blessing.In his early months in the job, Derek McInnes has been looking for a marquee performance. Now he has it. He was looking for a formation that worked and personnel that were big enough and bold enough to execute it and he got that, too. This was 3-0 going on more. Plenty more.The simplicity of their progression to the semi-final was a touch surreal. Neither of these were in particularly good form coming into this. They were both winning, yes, but they haven't been all that convincing. This season, in their last eight domestic features combined - all won, in fairness - there was only a goal in it at the end in seven of them. Both sides had got themselves into a cycle of missed chances and, at times, uncomfortable days.So the smart money was on a tight contest. Extra-time, maybe. Penalties? You wouldn't have ruled that out either. O'Neill is such a winning machine that many would have expected Celtic to find a way, somehow. So much for that.Few Old Firm games surprise you anymore, but this one was a gobsmacker. Rangers had all the intensity and all the togetherness. They had six players making their Old Firm debut from the start but if inexperience can be a challenge in this fixture then it was a challenge they met with gusto.McInnes and his driven and vastly superior players neutralised Celtic, shut them down, rendered them impotent. Celtic captain Callum McGregor lords it over days like this, but the supreme central midfielder was Dan Neil, not just in his outstanding goals but in the control and the leadership he exerted. With Nico Raskin beside him it was a no-contest in the middle of the pitch. James Penrice did a power of really good work in there, too.Camilo Duran, playing wide again instead of through the middle, has been one of the players of the season so far, but he hardly existed, totally bossed by Olwethu Makhanya - calm in the maelstrom, classy in nearly everything he did. Kasper Hogh needed a goal having scored in just one game in six - a hat-trick, albeit - but the record signing spent much of his day in Emmanuel Fernandez's pocket. He had no service and no sniff.Where did this come from? Lord knows, but it makes life very interesting now, not just in the destination of the League Cup - Rangers will be massive favourites against Aberdeen in their semi-final -  but in the race for the league title. McInnes might have hit on something substantial. The big task, of course, is to repeat that energy, that belief, that ruthlessness.You expected Celtic to stir and make a game of it, but they were never allowed to, in part because of their own awful shortcomings with the ball and in other part because Rangers didn't allow them to settle. They hunted them down, right from the opening minutes.A mood, of sorts, was set as early as the fourth minute when Sam Johnstone, Celtic's jumpy new goalkeeper, passed a clearance straight to Kevin Kelsy, who slashed it wide. Johnstone had been harried by Rangers' press, a big theme of the day. For Kelsy, it was a great chance to strike early, but if he failed then he made amends later on.Kelsy is only in the door, but he looks to have personality and desire. He was playing with Ryan Naderi, an oft-criticised striker, a player you hear constantly is not Rangers class. Naderi was one of the totems of the day, a work rate that never stopped, a constant menace in hunting and gathering. Naderi might have changed a few Rangers minds on Sunday.The opener was a microcosm; Naderi robbing Cameron Carter-Vickers, Kelsy then picking out Neil for a sumptuous finish. Rangers were physically and creatively on top, but there's always a feeling that one goal needed to become two to halt Celtic's assumed purple patch, a response that never came.That was the bizarre thing. Total authority for an entire game is a rare enough thing in this contest. Usually there's a spell when the team that's ahead has to weather some kind of storm. Celtic couldn't throw a bucket of water in Rangers' direction not to mind a tempest. When McInnes' side made it two it was only what they deserved.Penrice put in the cross, Naderi flicked it on and Kelsy banged in the volley. Neil's second and Rangers' third was a peach, a sign of confident uninhibited players enjoying themselves. The smallest of mercies for Celtic was that it stayed at three.The second part of this drama comes on Sunday, a league game that could not have been better set up had Eddie Hearn been involved in the promotion. Rangers looking to lay down another marker going to Celtic's home, full of 60,000 folk baying for revenge. Given some of the vile songs that were directed at O'Neill at Ibrox then McInnes is in for some treatment. Sadly, he's heard it all over before, as has O'Neill.McInnes was measured in the aftermath, more low-key than you might have expected and there was sense in that. This was one game and he knew it. They won nothing on the back of it and he knew that, too. Apart from, that is, precious momentum and self-belief and the knowledge of what their standard can be when they get it right. And on Sunday, they got it spectacularly right.

schema.headline: Tom English: Derek McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker

title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
description: There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Ang
body: There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC."Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg."But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve."The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said."We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference."Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail.BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold.Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built.But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit. BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target.

schema.headline: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC

title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
description: ByHayley Clarke and Beth RoseEducation reportersThere will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the go
body: ByHayley Clarke and Beth RoseEducation reportersThere will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing.Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said. Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet.But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition. Don't create another stick with which to beat head teachers when they are trying to do their very best to provide a healthy, balanced meal for those in our schools."He said schools needed "more investment" in catering facilities and in the "professional development" of school chefs to develop menus that "meet the ambitions" of the government.As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week. High-fibre bread will also become a requirement. Image caption, Under the new rules, all dishes must come with at least one portion of fruit or vegetablesBreakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes.Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals.The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted".Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils. One of those was Oasis Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes."The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said.Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis".Image caption, Farzana Ahmed welcomed both the new school food standards and the expansion of free school meals eligibilityAbout 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet.With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit, Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward."It's a really positive move," she said."We know how important a nutritional diet is to the wellbeing, to the behaviour, to the learning of our pupils."Working mum-of-three Kinza Butt said the free school meals her son was now getting at Blakenhale Juniors had lifted a "burden off the shoulders"."He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said."By the end of the day he used to be starving. But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well."Image caption, Newly-eligible parent Kinza is delighted her children can now have free school dinnersThe new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK.In Wales, new guidance will come into force by the end of the year with a greater focus on at least two portions of vegetables being offered every day, with only water, milk or plant-based drinks allowed for hydration.Scotland updated its legislation in 2020. It requires students to be offered at least two portions of vegetables and one portion of fruit every day and oily fish must be served at least once every three weeks.Northern Ireland last updated its regulations in 2007. They include providing bread everyday, without spread, and offering two portions of fruit and vegetables a day. It also stipulates that if beans or pulses form the protein part of a main course, another vegetable must be available.

schema.headline: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England

title: Meghan shares first glimpse of family life after return to UK
description: The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to  Instagram following their return to the UK. The 34-second clip, which
body: The Duchess of Sussex has shared a glimpse of family life in footage posted to  Instagram following their return to the UK. The 34-second clip, which features Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go, begins with Meghan, along with her husband Prince Harry, walking along a country path as she turns and says "come on, you". UK flag and heart emojis are shown throughout the video, which also shows their son Archie running towards deer as their daughter Lilibet rides her bike. Another clip sees Harry fishing with the children as their dog walks alongside the water. It's the first time the Duchess has posted her family on her Instagram grid since the Sussexes returned from from the US after living in California. It is unclear when, or where, the footage posted on Sunday afternoon was taken, external, but one clip shows a pair of wellington boots walking on the spot in a puddle and the children also appear to be in waterproof boots as they head toward the deer.   The UK has had a wet start to September after experiencing its hottest summer on record.The post offers a rare glimpse into the lives of seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. Whereas Meghan does occasionally show the couple's children on social media, their faces are often obscured as they are photgraphed from behind or their faces are hidden by their parents.  Alongside all the outside footage, there is also a moment showing a child's feet in front of an open fire. Last month, a spokesman for the Sussexes would not confirm the family's arrival in the UK, but did say they were bringing their dogs, Mia and Pula,with them. The couple adopted a black Labrador retriever several years ago, which is seen several times in the clip. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020. They have not returned to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals. It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area, and Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in a school. Last week, a spokesperson for both the Duke and Duchess said the couple were surprised by a letter send by the Prince's father, King Charles III, clarifying they would remain non-working royals. The spokesperson said the couple "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".The letter, sent on behalf of the King, spelt out the non-working royal status of Prince Harry and Meghan.They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.

schema.headline: Meghan shares first glimpse of family life after return to UK

title: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
description: US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts."You have a lot of very neg
body: US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts."You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC that staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI  – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.On one hand, the sector is seen as a huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.In August, OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.The Trump administration argues that the US must maintain global tech dominance as a matter of national security, though it has admitted a need for vigilance around the risks posed by the emerging technology. The weekend call by major AI executives sparked discussion in Washington, where lawmakers are facing pressure to address those potential risks around rapid AI developments. On Sunday, Speaker Mike Johnson, the top House Republican, urged caution about rushing AI regulation during an appearance on CNN's Jake Tapper on State of the Union,  arguing it could "smother American innovation"."If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American," he said. "So, we've got to have balance. We've got to have steady hands at the wheel."Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries argued for "decisive action" by lawmakers.He told George Stephanopoulos on ABC's This Week that the US should slow down "the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely".Responding to recent comments from the AI industry, tech investor David Sacks, who serves on Trump's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, called on the companies to police themselves. "Stop pretending you need anyone else's permission," he posted on X."So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it... Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it."Still, there is at least some cross-party consensus on AI regulation. In July, a group of House Democrats and Republicans introduced the Frontier Act, a bipartisan bill that seeks to establish a national safety and oversight framework for AI."Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway," Rep Lori Trahan, a Massachusetts Democrat who co-authored the bill, wrote on X this week. "It's past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job."

schema.headline: Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down

title: Spanish Grand Prix: How VSC cost Lando Norris race win - and should F1 change the rules?
description: Lando Norris says he was "insanely unlucky" to lose what seemed like a certain win in the Spanish Grand Prix because of the timing of a virtual safety
body: Lando Norris says he was "insanely unlucky" to lose what seemed like a certain win in the Spanish Grand Prix because of the timing of a virtual safety car.McLaren's Norris was leading comfortably when the VSC was called, seconds after he had passed the pit lane entry.That allowed Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen to pit under the VSC, saving time, while the caution period ended before Norris could make it around to the pits again.Of the VSC, Norris said: "It is a rule that should not define a whole race.""I was the only one on the whole grid that didn't get the chance to do the pit stop," he said. "That's just unfortunate."There's been plenty of times where I've gained from it in the past and times where I've lost from it, and it's racing, but never when fighting for a win."So, it's probably one of the first times a win has been lost simply because of it."After taking pole position with a lap his team principal Andrea Stella described as "a masterpiece", Norris was leading Antonelli by more than six seconds after 13 laps in Madrid.He had just passed the pit entry at the end of lap 14 when a VSC was called because Lance Stroll's Aston Martin had stopped in the run-off area at Turn 20, while  Antonelli and Verstappen were far enough behind to pit.The VSC, which controls all cars to a specified maximum speed, then ended shortly before Norris completed the next lap, at the end of which he pitted.Because a stop under the VSC costs 11 seconds less race time than one under green-flag conditions, Norris lost sufficient time that Antonelli and Verstappen were able to pass him.Norris lost a further five seconds because of problems with his two right-hand side tyres at the stop and emerged from the pits more than 15 seconds behind Antonelli and more than nine adrift of Verstappen.He caught the Red Bull before the end of the race but as overtaking was virtually impossible on the new Madring street circuit, he was stuck in third place.Race-winner Antonelli, who extended his championship lead to 81 points, acknowledged Norris' bad fortune. "If I have to be realistic and honest, today we didn't deserve to win," he said. "Lando deserved to win, and so I think our result was probably P2 or even P3."The short duration of the VSC in this case was exactly why Norris was railing against the situation.Every other driver in the field had the opportunity to decide whether to pit or not - the only driver not given that option was Norris.The pit lane entry is before the final corner at the Madring, and Norris was in the last corner when it was called.The VSC ended when Norris was in Turn 21, the corner before the pit entry, on lap 15. Antonelli, having stopped, was behind him in Turn 19.On most circuits, Norris would have had a chance to pass Verstappen and perhaps even do the same to Antonelli before the end, given his pace advantage on the day, but as Antonelli put it: "In the race, you're just stuck behind."Norris was withering in his criticism of the track layout, saying: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, 'Mint.'" But he did say there was "a lot of opportunity" to improve it for next year.After the race, one question asked of McLaren was whether pitting on the following lap was the best idea, or should Norris have stayed out?Norris said: "I had to come in at the end of the lap because it was the only chance."It was still effectively some pit loss, (but) the fact that everyone's kind of on colder tyres and you're still minimising the pit loss."The medium tyre (on which Norris had started the race) was destroyed and the hard tyre (to which Antonelli and Verstappen switched) was amazing."But the pace was very, very strong and on the hard tyre... I know they were stuck (behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who stayed out under the VSC), we caught up 13, 14 seconds or more, almost. So, plenty of positives. A day full of positives, just one thing let it all down."McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "We considered staying out, but you have to accept the fact that now you are on relatively used medium tyres. And the people behind you will be on new hard. So you're never going to open a gap on people on new hard."The other question was whether McLaren would have been wise to anticipate that the race director would call the VSC and pit Norris before it was deployed.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "In hindsight, that would have been a good idea."But he pointed out that, in the moment, it would have come with risks. The long pit lane at the Madring - the longest on the calendar - meant a pit stop cost a lot of time.Stella said: "I would have to review with my engineers, see whether it was kind of obvious that it would end up in a virtual safety car. Therefore, you try to anticipate or not."Here, the problem is that you need to be extremely careful, because it's 27 seconds if you don't pit under a virtual safety car."So if you get it wrong, it would be extremely penalising. From the lead, you pit unnecessarily, and now you have lost the victory."So a good rule is to respond to what is a fact, to what is the real condition of the circuit."But we will definitely take a look as to whether in these conditions it was just simply, you know, obvious that he would end up in a virtual safety car. I cannot answer at the moment."After the race, Norris and Verstappen said this kind of scenario had been discussed by drivers many times with governing body the FIA."I think there's always probably some cons to doing it, but it's tough," Norris said."I've won from it in the past, I've lost from it in the past. Over the course of a season, it's hard to know if it's a good thing or a bad thing."It probably equals out over time. Of course, it just hurts more, the fact that I lose a win. You know, there's literally nothing I could do as a driver today to do a better job."Verstappen said: "We'll probably talk about it in the next briefing and see if there is anything that can be done."Stella added: "Perhaps there's a wider reflection that the Formula 1 community should apply as to whether you keep things like they are or you introduce ways of maintaining more fairness."Offering the personal opinion. I'm puzzled myself as to what's right."Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions? So, for instance, the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap? Or you just keep it in the hands of the gods, and sometimes you are lucky, sometimes you are not. I'm not sure myself."But in general, there's the right place to have this sort of conversation, which is the Strategy Advisory Committee (SAC). And this is a topic that may be added to the agenda and discussed over there."But if there is to be a change, it will have to be a change that goes through the SAC, then the F1 Commission, and then we'll have to go at some stage to the sporting regulations."But I would envisage that this is a relatively lengthy process, unless there's a big push from F1, from the institutions, FIA or F1, to say, like, 'we need to make this different'."

schema.headline: Spanish Grand Prix: How VSC cost Lando Norris race win - and should F1 change the rules?

title: Referees body admits error of judgement over Erling Haaland derby winner
description: The Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's Manchester City winner against Manchester
body: The Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's Manchester City winner against Manchester United.As City celebrated a remarkable derby victory over Manchester United, there were questions as to whether Haaland's winning goal should have stood in a match fraught with controversy.The striker scored in the 60th minute at Old Trafford, turning home at the back post from Josko Gvardiol's cross before it was disallowed on the field for offside.Following intervention from the video assistant referee, the goal was awarded - the Norwegian ruled to have been played onside by Patrick Dorgu's boot.But there was debate as to whether the offside Enzo Fernandez, diving at the ball in a more central position than Haaland, was interfering with play.In a statement, Pro Ref said: "It was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective."However, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review."Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place."United defender Lisandro Martinez said it was an "injustice" while boss Michael Carrick said he was "confused" by the decision.The goal came after City had gone down to 10 men in the first half when Phil Foden was shown a straight red card for kicking out at United captain Bruno Fernandes.Foden was dismissed by referee Michael Oliver on 23 minutes after kicking the midriff of Fernandes while he was on the turf.When Haaland's goal was ruled out as offside on the field, few questioned the decision as the City striker looked to have drifted beyond United's defensive line.The lines drawn by the VAR showed Haaland to be onside thanks to Dorgu's boot. But it was the positioning and involvement of Fernandez that left many pundits astounded and unsure if it was a legitimate goal.Gvardiol's cross took a slight deflection off the boot of Dorgu before finding its way to Haaland at the back post, while Fernandez was clearly attempting a diving header in the middle of the six-yard box but he did not touch the ball.Fernandez appeared to be in an offside position, ahead of Dorgu's boot, but VAR deemed it to be a legitimate goal as he did not touch the ball while United defender Martinez was also closing in.The Premier League Match Centre said on X: "VAR checked the referee's call of no goal for offside - and determined that Haaland was in an onside position and recommended that the goal was awarded."The VAR also deemed that while in an offside position, Fernandez didn't play the ball."Dale Johnson, BBC Sport football issues correspondentThe curiosity about this incident is that the goal was initially disallowed for the wrong reason. Haaland was flagged offside when he shouldn't have been.But as it turned out, the goal should have been ruled out because Fernandez was offside.There is one key part of the offside law which applies to Fernandez here. A player is offside if they are:"Clearly attempting to play a ball which is close when this action impacts on an opponent."Both parts of that clause must be met. It is possible for a player in an offside position to attempt to play a ball and not commit an offence – there must be impact on an opponent too.As the ball came in, Fernandez threw himself to try to head it, with Martinez directly behind him.Video assistant referee Matt Donohue should ask himself if Fernandez's action would have influenced Martinez.In other words: If Fernandez had not jumped for the attempted header, would Martinez have made a different decision over playing the ball?If the ball had been out of reach for Fernandez, or for Martinez, then there is an argument to give the goal.And also: There would have been no offside had Fernandez made no attempt to play the ball.But he did. And as it went just a yard in front of Martinez too, it is very difficult to argue Fernandez did not commit an offside offence.There is also an argument that the actions of Fernandez influence the positioning of goalkeeper Senne Lammens.However, the goal was originally ruled out for offside against Haaland - which was incorrect. So that decision had to be overturned. And then, the VAR should have sent referee Michael Oliver to the monitor for the subjective offence by Fernandez.It would have created the odd situation where a disallowed goal was reviewed to remain ruled out - but this is what should have happened.It was a clear offside offence by Fernandez and will go down as a VAR mistake.Was the VAR too concerned with a possible touch by Fernandez?If so, did the VAR forget that Fernandez was offside, and not consider the subjective offence? It seems to be the most logical explanation.A similar thing happened in a game between Arsenal and Brentford in February 2023 when a goal by an offside Christian Norgaard was not disallowed.With Haaland's goal settling the match, United were unsurprisingly disappointed by the decision."I think it was offside," said Martinez. "And what I can't understand is the rules. I want to be calm now, I want to control myself. "It's so hard because you lose a derby, you lose three points at home, and every season they're [referees] coming to our club, they explain for one hour the rules, and they look so confident with that, and then after [there are] five or six people doing these kind of mistakes in the Premier League - it's unacceptable."It's the best league in the world, you have the best teams in the world, the best players in the world, and now we have to go home with this injustice."United boss Carrick also expressed his confusion."We put things in place in the game now, we have people in offices with all the screens for this decision," he said. "It's more worrying about if that's the interpretation of football now. If that's the interpretation of not interfering in the game now, that's really worrying for me. It's a staggering explanation."The decision isn't going to change the season, but it's had a major impact on the game."Wayne Rooney, part of the BBC's MOTD2 team, said: "Surely it's offside. Martinez is impacted by Fernandez's movement, and he is offside."Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I think we'll see some sort of apology from the referee's association, there's no doubt Fernandez is playing that ball and is trying to put off Martinez. I think it's one they'll recognising they got wrong."Micah Richards added: "I think it's been a bad day for referees. They got the Foden decision wrong and the Fernandez decision wrong. I think they got it so wrong but I don't think it takes anything away from City's performance."Meanwhile, City boss Maresca said: "I think it was onside clearly so it's good."The goal came after a first half laced with controversy, with Foden shown a straight red for kicking out at midfielder Fernandes.City midfielder Foden picked up the ball wide on the right-hand side in his own half and was closed down by Fernandes, who tripped him.Foden then kicked out at the body of the Portuguese midfielder while on the ground and was shown a straight red card by the referee.Replays showed that Fernandes kicked Foden in the back first, before the England international retaliated.The incident was checked by the VAR, who confirmed the on-field decision; Fernandes was not shown a card.Pundits were divided on whether Foden should have seen red and whether Fernandes was the man at fault.Former Manchester United forward Rooney did not believe it was a red, saying "it was more of a flick or a gesture, than a kick out".Neville said he was "surprised" Fernandes did not receive a booking for his role while Roy Keane said the fault lay with the Portuguese midfielder."Foden gets up and reacts obviously, so he's sent off," he said. "Fernandes catches him and gives him a little kick. I guess it's classed as violent. But Fernandes is the one who is violent here, I don't think Foden should have a red card."Dale Johnson, BBC Sport's issues correspondent, said: "The referee and VAR would have to deem it violent conduct rather than just petulance from Fernandes."The guidance changed some years ago to factor that in, so David Beckham's kick on Diego Simeone in the 1998 World Cup would not result in a sending off today."It looked to me like there was little to no contact from Fernandes, and if there was it was limited force and wasn't followed through."So Bruno's act would be seen as a yellow card offence, which the VAR obviously can't get involved in."

title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporterUpdated 06:55 BSTElla can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing."I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing."It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."Image source, EllaImage caption, Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards)Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners. So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for: Worn, chipped or flattened teethHeadaches or facial pain in the morningJaw stiffnessDisrupted sleep and daytime tirednessIncreased tooth sensitivityEarache or pain near the temples without infectionTeeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".'A way of releasing some of the stress' Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth."If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake. "I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me."I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.Image source, EllaImage caption, After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improvedEven though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months."Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time."Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.Image source, Simon CoveImage caption, A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teethWhile you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai."Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening."It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again."That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition.And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains."Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion." Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition."We know this in animals, and our preliminary research is showing it in humans," he says. "By working our jaw muscles we are stimulating blood flow to the brain."But teeth grinding can also cause chronic pain, which can have a huge impact on your daily life.What is the treatment for bruxism? Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person."We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach." How best to tackle it? These things might help: Mouthguard to wear at night to protect your teethIf linked to sleep apnoea, devices such as a CPAP machine or a mandibular advancement device (MAD) to help keep the airway openPhysiotherapyTalking therapies such as CBTLifestyle changes to help reduce stress and improve sleep such as exercise, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and eating healthierFor severe cases Botox is an option, but it's rarely available on the NHSAlong with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries."Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues discussed in this story?

schema.headline: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?

title: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
description: Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's econom
body: Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said.Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March."These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances". Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me. "But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back."One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March.Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date."That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy."There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions."It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this."Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box".Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions".Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending.She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10."A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals."Jenrick said Delo and Harborne  - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda".Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". Delo had written in the newspaper the day prior that he wanted to enable Reform to put up a "fair fight at the next election.The £72m from the two is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year.Delo was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMex, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.Reform's fundraising has come under scrutiny in recent months. This includes police announcing an investigation over allegations the party broke foreign funding laws in a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.The party's leader Nigel Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m gift he received from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.Both Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing in both instances.

schema.headline: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says

title: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, Andy Burnham urges
description: The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting with some of the UK's biggest bosses.The prime minist
body: The UK needs a "culture shift" in how it does business, Andy Burnham has said ahead of a meeting with some of the UK's biggest bosses.The prime minister said those who take risks in business should be backed by government and local leaders should have the power to work with businesses.The current Labour government has been criticised for increasing costs for businesses, such as with the employer national insurance and minimum wage changes under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.Downing Street said Burnham will meet with the chief executives of BP, Shell, HSBC, Morrisons, Sainsbury's, BT, Vodafone, Rolls-Royce, and several others at Number 10.Ahead of the meeting, Burnham said he would give people "the confidence that if they have a great idea, they'll get all the support they need to bring it to life"."When local leaders have the tools to get things done and government works in partnership with business, you can pull in investment, create jobs and transform communities," he said.He added the government would be "a partner for growth to make every part of Britain better off".Burnham will host a reception for the business community where local leaders are invited before a private engagement with senior chief executives at Downing Street on Monday evening.The meeting comes as higher borrowing costs in the UK and other countries present problems for governments looking to spend money on business support or investment.Official data revealed a surprise boost in the economy in July partly driven by artificial intelligence (AI) investment, though experts expect growth to slow in the months ahead due to high energy prices.The US-Israel war with Iran has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices, affecting households and businesses.This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.The expectation of higher interest rates, as well as competition for debt from AI firms looking to spend money on development, has driven up the cost of government borrowing in many countries.However, many argue the UK has a particular problem with high government debt. The UK yield for 10-year bonds, a key measure of government debt costs, is higher than countries such as the US, France, and Japan.Experts say this is due to several factors affecting investor confidence in the UK, such as multiple prime ministers, chancellors and policy U-turns over a short period.In an interview with the BBC last week, Chancellor John Healey called for a restoration of "confidence about Britain" despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.Others have argued that the Labour government has created its own problems by increasing costs for businesses.Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "The way for the prime minister to get businesses thriving, delivering jobs and driving growth is to cut their taxes."Labour's jobs tax and employer red tape have been devastating for businesses. The consequence has been a drying-up of the jobs market, weaker investment and businesses facing ever greater costs."

schema.headline: 'Culture shift' needed in how UK does business, Andy Burnham urges

title: First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff
description: The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss ways of "working more closely", including on con
body: The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss ways of "working more closely", including on constitutional issues.It will be the first face-to-face meeting between the three nationalist leaders since Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth took office in May.Ap Iorwerth will host the SNP's leader John Swinney and Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill on Monday morning. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald will also attend.He will hold further talks with Swinney in the afternoon with both men expected to sign an agreement on "future collaboration in areas of shared interest".For the first time since devolution began Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.A Plaid spokesperson said ap Iorwerth's meeting with Swinney, O'Neill and McDonald was "an opportunity for the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Féin to come together and talk about how we can work more closely on the issues that matter to people across our nations"."Following the historic Senedd election in Wales and the changing political landscape across these islands, there is a strong case for practical political cooperation on areas including energy, the economy and our relationship with Europe, as well as on the wider political and constitutional questions facing our nations and on the right to self-determination," they added.Swinney believed their was "undeniable" momentum behind constitutional change."Every nation across these islands is standing at a moment of incredible constitutional opportunity," he said."There is a growing consensus that the Westminster system simply is not fit for purpose and does not work for ordinary people. "Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accepted that himself - and the people of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have made it clear at the ballot box."The meetings come days after the matter of Scottish independence resurfaced in the Commons.During Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham appeared to indicate a second referendum could be held in Scotland if there was clear public support for a vote. He compared the situation to the conditions for a border poll in Northern Ireland explaining the Good Friday Agreement made clear a border poll would be "considered by the Northern Ireland Secretary when there is a clear consensus in the country, when public opinion has changed to the point where the call has to be considered"."I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland," he added.The apparent softening in tone was welcomed by Swinney before Burnham clarified that another Scottish referendum remained "off limits". A referendum on Scottish independence in September 2014 saw the country vote to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.Ap Iorwerth was appointed the first non-Labour first minister of Wales after May's Senedd election.Whilst he has ruled out pushing for a referendum on Welsh independence during his party's first term in government, he has said he wants to lead a "national conversation" about the issue.His government intends to set up a national commission to "lay the foundations" for future plans for Welsh independence.In the meantime, Welsh ministers are also asking for extra powers to be transferred to Wales, including over policing and youth justice.Burnham has said he is "open" to the idea. In Northern Ireland, the first and deputy first minister have identical powers and responsibilities and the DUP's Emma Little-Pengelly is the deputy first minister.Little-Pengelly of unionist party the DUP criticised O'Neill for attending. Monday's talks are likely to cover the way the devolved nations are funded by the UK government.Welsh ministers have long called for the Barnett funding formula to be reformed, claiming it disadvantages Wales.However, it is argued Scotland does well from the formula.Before he became prime minister Burnham made the case for change, but on his recent visit to Wales he played down the prospect of reform.The devolved leaders will meet the prime minister next month. The UK government said: "The prime minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the union."Welsh Conservatives leader Darren Millar said: "Instead of obsessing about independence, the first minister should be focused on dealing with the crisis engulfing the Welsh NHS and the declining standards in Welsh schools."Reform UK Wales said: "Plaid Cymru is showing its true colours by meeting with Sinn Féin and the Scottish separatists."

schema.headline: First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to meet in Cardiff

title: Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station
description: A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security official
body: A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through.No casualties were reported after the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said. Johnson and other European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on a different train on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.Russia said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly, the target of this drone could have been the diplomatic train".In a statement, it said the train "had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes".It also said an evacuation order for passengers on the hit train had been given "just 15 minutes"  before the strike by a Russian jet-propelled drone.The railway authority also said former CIA chief David Petraeus had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the drone strike.Both Ukrainian and Polish authorities said the Russian drone had struck 2km from the Polish border.Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who had also attended the conference in Kyiv, told the BBC passengers on board his train had been told to prepare for evacuation before subsequently being allowed to continue their journey."On the train I was on we received order to prepare evacuation after it had stopped. But after a number of minutes we were informed that it was clear and we could proceed," he said.That train then safely arrived at Poland's border station in Dorohusk.Some reports have suggested Bildt was on the same train as Johnson, but the former UK prime minister has not confirmed any details.  Johnson wrote on X: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning.He said this was "the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day - even on civilian railways" and urged Kyiv's allies to urgently provide Ukrainians "the air defences they need".Ukraine has made repeated pleas to its allies - particularly the US - to provide more interceptors to defend against daily Russian attacks that increasingly use fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones.Russia appears to be escalating its war against Ukraine by targeting trains, railway depots, petrol stations and border crossings.Earlier this week, two people were killed when Russian drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.Also this week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine. Six Ukrzaliznytsia employees were killed after a depot was struck n Kyiv at the start of the month. In January, Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead.The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.European countries are also blaming Russia for suspicious incidents on their territory.Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd".There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.

title: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters

body: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth. When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly. "All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked."They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'. "And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'. "At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook."'Remember me?' she asked. Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result."I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match". "I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister. "This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters. "It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be." Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago. It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters. "We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know." Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents."Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says."Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began."We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together. "There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says."I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

schema.headline: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
